A  In the early 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus embarked on a series of experiments that would make him one of the founders of the scientific study of memory. Lacking a laboratory or a team of assistants, he used the only participant who was reliably available: himself. To avoid the complication that some words are easier to remember than others because of their meaning or associations, he constructed more than two thousand 'nonsense syllables', each consisting of a consonant, a vowel and another consonant, such as DAX or BOK. He then memorised lists of these syllables and tested how much he retained after intervals ranging from twenty minutes to a month.

B  Rather than simply counting how many items he could recall, Ebbinghaus measured how much time he saved when relearning a list compared with learning it the first time. The results, published in 1885, revealed a striking pattern. Forgetting was steepest shortly after learning: a substantial proportion of the material was lost within the first hour or so. After that, the rate of loss slowed considerably, so that the decline between the first and the sixth day was far smaller than the decline in the first hour. Plotted on a graph, this relationship became known as the forgetting curve, and it has been reproduced many times since, including in a careful replication published in 2015.

C  Ebbinghaus also noticed something of more practical value. When he spread his study sessions over several days rather than concentrating them into a single sitting, he needed fewer repetitions in total to master a list. This phenomenon, now called the spacing effect, is among the most robust findings in experimental psychology. It has been demonstrated with children and older adults, with vocabulary, mathematics and motor skills, and even in non-human animals. In a large study published in 2008, researchers found that the ideal gap between study sessions depends on how long the learner needs to remember the material: the longer the desired retention, the longer the optimal interval.

D  A closely related finding concerns the value of testing. Many students treat tests purely as a way of measuring knowledge, but a substantial body of research suggests that the act of retrieving information from memory actually strengthens it. In a well-known experiment from 2006, students who read a passage once and then practised recalling it remembered considerably more a week later than students who spent the same time rereading the passage repeatedly, even though the rereading group predicted that they would remember more. When retrieval practice is combined with spacing, the benefits appear to be greater still.

E  These insights have been built into a variety of study tools. In the 1970s, the German journalist Sebastian Leitner proposed a system in which flashcards are sorted into a series of boxes: cards answered correctly move to a box that is reviewed less often, while cards answered incorrectly return to the first box. Modern spaced-repetition software applies the same logic automatically, using algorithms to schedule each item for review shortly before it is likely to be forgotten. Such programs are particularly popular among language learners and medical students, who must retain very large numbers of individual facts.

F  Why, then, do so many learners continue to rely on cramming? One reason is that massed practice produces rapid short-term gains that feel like genuine learning. Information that has just been read seems familiar, and this sense of fluency is easily mistaken for durable knowledge. Spaced study, in contrast, involves more effortful recall and more frequent experiences of having forgotten something, which can feel discouraging. Psychologists refer to such techniques as 'desirable difficulties': strategies that slow apparent progress but improve long-term retention. Persuading students that struggle can be a sign of effective learning remains one of the central challenges for educators.

Roughly 40 per cent of all languages are considered endangered, meaning that children are no longer learning them, or are learning them in declining numbers. When the last fluent speakers of such a language die, a unique system of grammar, vocabulary and oral tradition disappears with them.

B  Languages rarely die because their speakers simply lose interest. More often, decline follows a combination of economic, political and social pressures. Speakers of minority languages may find that employment and education are available only in a dominant language, and parents may decide, often for understandable reasons, that their children's prospects depend on speaking it well. In many cases, governments actively suppressed minority languages: in Hawaii, for example, a law passed in 1896 required English to be the medium of instruction in schools, and within a few generations Hawaiian had almost ceased to be learned as a first language. By the early 1980s, fewer than fifty children were thought to speak it natively.

C  The case most often cited as evidence that decline can be reversed is that of Hebrew. For centuries Hebrew had been used for prayer, scholarship and writing, but it was not the everyday spoken language of any community. In the late nineteenth century, Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others promoted its use in daily life, coining new words for modern concepts and insisting on speaking Hebrew at home. Today it has millions of native speakers. The idea was adopted in Hawaii in 1984, and children who began in Hawaiian-language preschools were later able to continue their education in Hawaiian, in some cases up to university level. In many cases, governments actively suppressed minority languages: in Hawaii, for example, a law passed in 1896 required English to be the medium of instruction in schools, and within a few generations Hawaiian had almost ceased to be learned as a first language. By the early 1980s, fewer than fifty children were thought to speak it natively.

C  The case most often cited as evidence that decline can be reversed is that of Hebrew. For centuries Hebrew had been used for prayer, scholarship and writing, but it was not the everyday spoken language of any community. In the late nineteenth century, Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others promoted its use in daily life, coining new words for modern concepts and insisting on speaking Hebrew at home. Today it has millions of native speakers. I would argue, however, that this example is less transferable than is often supposed, since the revival depended on an unusual combination of circumstances, including a large population highly motivated to adopt a shared language and, eventually, the support of a state.

D  Communities with fewer resources have developed other strategies. In New Zealand in the early 1980s, Māori communities established 'language nests', preschools in which elders spoke only Māori with young children. The idea was adopted in Hawaii in 1984, and children who began in Hawaiian-language preschools were later able to continue their education in Hawaiian, in some cases up to university level. In California, where many indigenous languages have very few speakers left, a 'master-apprentice' approach pairs a fluent elder with a younger adult learner, who spend many hours together each week carrying out ordinary activities entirely in the language.

E  Even languages that have lost all their native speakers may be brought back into use. The last person to have grown up speaking Manx, the Celtic language of the Isle of Man, died in 1974, but enthusiasts had recorded him and other elderly speakers, and today a small primary school on the island teaches children through the medium of Manx. Such cases demonstrate that documentation, including recordings, dictionaries and grammars, can serve not merely as a memorial but as the basis for renewal. Critics sometimes dismiss revived languages as artificial, but this objection seems to me unconvincing: all languages are shaped by the choices of their speakers.

F  The single most important factor in the survival of a language, most researchers agree, is whether it is passed from parents to children in the home. Schools, broadcasting and official status can support this process but cannot replace it. Revitalisation is therefore not only a technical challenge but also a matter of attitudes: parents must believe that the language is worth transmitting, and young people must see it as relevant to their lives rather than as a relic of the past. Where those conditions are met, even severely endangered languages have shown that decline is not inevitable.
